title: A ghostly presence lingers in Louisiana's Old State Capitol. Who is it?
excerpt: Workers have reported hearing footsteps throughout the building, with the exception of one room.
content:
As is the case with legends, no one knows when congressman Pierre Aurélien Couvillion became the ghost of Louisiana's Old State Capitol. But someone at some time tagged the Marksville legislator as the presence who walked the Old Capitol's floors after hours.

Couvillion served as a Louisiana state senator from 1846 to 1848. The popular tale is that he died from a heart attack on the Senate chamber floor during a heated debate.

As the story goes, Couvillion learned that some of his fellow legislators were securing financial favors from members of the banking industry at taxpayers’ expense, and he became so angry that his heart couldn't take it.

“But someone did some research a few years ago and found that Pierre died of a heart attack in his home in Marksville,” said Mary Durusau, the museum's director. “So, they wrote this bio about him, and I wish I knew where it came from. Sadly, it's just a typed bio, and there's no attribution of where it came from or anything. But it says he had a heart attack on Nov. 19, 1851, at his home in Avoyelles Parish.”

Couvillion story debunked

Durusau acknowledges that there's a lot of vagueness surrounding the sources of Couvillion's story, but his time in the Legislature was officially recorded in the Louisiana State Legislature Senate Directory.

“He died two years after he left the Legislature, so he didn't die in the Capitol,” Durusau said. “And he's buried in Avoyelles Parish.”

Even if Couvillion had, indeed, died on the Senate floor, it would have happened in New Orleans. Construction on the Old Capitol in Baton Rouge didn't start until 1847. 

Lawmakers didn’t convene there until Jan. 21, 1850, after Couvillion had left office.

Footsteps after hours

Yet the debunking of Couvillion's presence doesn't mean the museum has given up the ghost. Workers have reported hearing its footsteps throughout the building.

Well, with the exception of one room. 

“The only place I didn't see or hear anything was in the Senate chamber when I was working there,” said Carl Smith, the Old Capitol's former maintenance supervisor and chief maintenance engineer.

Smith now supervises maintenance at the Capitol Park Museum, where he's experienced nothing paranormal. For most of Smith’s nine years working in the Old State Capitol, staff called the ghost Pierre.

“I never saw anything face to face, but I did see shadows. I don't know who it was, but I heard something there,” Smith said. “I don't think it's Sarah Morgan,” Smith said.

In the museum’s four-dimensional theatrical program, “The Ghost of the Castle,” Civil War diarist Sarah Morgan appears as an apparition to tell the story of the castlelike capitol that stands on land donated by her family.

Who is it?

Durusau offers a few suggestions on who the ghost in the Old State Capitol might be.

“The Capitol had a pond on its grounds in the 1800s,” she said. “It's said that people threw their valuables in the pond during the Civil War to protect them from being taken by the Union Army. The idea was that they would fish their valuables out after the war.”

When the pond was drained after the war, workers found a skeleton among the soggy valuables.

“No one knows the identity of the skeleton,” Durusau said. “But, who knows? Maybe it's that person's ghost who is haunting the Capitol.”

She adds that the Union used the building as a prison and hospital during the Civil War, and perhaps the spirit could belong to one of the soldiers who died there. Then she floats another idea.

“You know, Henry Watkins Allen is buried on the grounds,” Durusau said. “A lot of people don't know this, because his grave looks like a big monument.”

Allen is the namesake for the city of Port Allen. His grave is topped by a rose-colored obelisk situated where the museum's sculpted lawn borders the corner of North Boulevard and River Road.

The obelisk also marks the third grave site for Allen, the former Confederate general-turned-Louisiana governor who was initially buried in the Mexico City National Cemetery and Memorial upon his death in 1866.

Ten years later, he was relocated to Lafayette Cemetery in New Orleans, and in 1885 — 19 years after his death — his remains were moved to their final resting place at the Old State Capitol.

“So, if anyone has a reason to be disgruntled, it would be him,” Durusau said.

Don't ask about Pierre

Meanwhile, the museum has removed the prompt, “Ask about Pierre, our ghost,” from its brochures. Also gone is a display once dedicated to Couvillion.

But that hasn't stopped visitors from inquiring about the Avoyelles legislator.

“It comes up a lot,” Durusau said.

No matter the confusion over identity, Smith knows something is there. He's watched paranormal investigative groups explore the castle through the years, but he didn't need their affirmation.

“You try to brush it off as your mind is playing tricks on you, but I was freaked out all the time,” he said. “Most of the time it was after hours or early, early in the morning when I was opening up the building, and everything was still dark. And it happened one time in the basement and a couple of times in the House chamber.”

Smith would hear distinct footsteps and doors opening and closing, and out of the corner of his eye, he'd see the movement of shadow figures.

“I saw someone walking into the House chamber, and I went to check it out,” he said. “But no one was there.”

Smith said the paranormal activity escalated when Gov. Mike Foster was inaugurated on the Old Capitol's grounds in 1996. Foster chose the spot in honor of his grandfather, Murphy Foster, who was inaugurated governor in the same location in 1892.

Maybe it was the sudden influx of people that stirred the activity, but the ghost has been a mainstay. Smith recalls a co-worker telling him about standing in the vicinity of doors and hearing them open and close, while seeing none of them physically move.

However, Smith's most bizarre ghost experience happened in the museum's basement.

“This sounds weird, but the bathroom stall door in the basement felt like it was coming off the hinges,” he said. “So, I put it back on the hinges, tightened it up real tight, and I kind of tugged on it to make sure it was on there.”

The next morning, Smith discovered the door had once again come off its hinges.

“So I fixed it again,” he said. “I'm thinking maybe the screws are rusted. So, I tightened them really tight, and I tugged on them and said, 'OK, it ain't going nowhere.'”

But on the third morning …

“I came in and it was down again,” Smith said. “I said, 'Well, I guess we're just going to leave this one off.”

And with that, the ghost formerly known as Pierre won the battle of the basement bathroom door.
